### Introduction
## Part A - Arithmetic Operations

```{r}
a <- 17
b <- 5

add <- a + b
sub <- a - b
multiply <- a * b
divide <- a / b

add
sub
multiply
divide
```

When I run the code, it displays all the operations on screen because I assigned values to the variables and I used arithmetic operations on those said variables.

```{r}
a <- 17
b <- 5

modulo <- a %% b
integer <- a %/% b

```
In the modulo, it takes the remainder of the answer, that is why it is 2. In the integer part, it is 3 because it divides the numbers.

```{r}
a <- 2 ^ 10
a
```
When I assign this value to a, it prints out 2 raised to 10.

Question #1: Run 17/5, 17 %% 5, and 17 %/% 5 side by side. In your own words, explain how these three results relate to each other mathematically.

17/5 prints out 3 since 17 divided by 5 is 3. For the modulo, it prints out 2 since 2 is the remainder. For the %/% is prints out 3 since it also divides. Three of them corellates with each other since they are also almost the same operations.

Question #2: Predict the output of 10 %% 3 and 10 %/% 3 before running the code. Were you correct? If not, explain what you misunderstood.

Yes I was correct, because it is simple division with remainder.

## Part B — Basic Data Types: typeof(), class(), and mode()
R has several basic data types: double (decimal numbers), integer, character (text), logical (TRUE/FALSE), and complex. typeof() reports the low-level storage type; class() reports the object’s class, which is sometimes more general.

```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i 

typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)

```
When I use typeof(), it check whether or not the value is an integer, double, character, etc... This is a good way to check what type of value is assigned to the variable.

```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i 

class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)
```
When using class(), it checks if the value is numeric, integer, character, logical, complex, etc... This is also a good way to check what the class of the value is easily.

```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i 

mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```
Mode checks what type of data the variable is storing.

Question #3): x <- 42 and y <- 42L look almost identical, but typeof(x) and typeof(y) give different answers. Explain the difference in your own words.

The difference is very common since x only contains 42 while y contains 42L, while x is a numeric, y on the other hand contains a letter.

Question #4: Is typeof() ever different from class() and from mode() for the same object? Look at your results above and explain any case where this happens (or, if you did not see one, explain what you would expect for a matrix or factor).

typeof() checks the internal base type of a variable, class() checks the abstract type of the variable, and mode() is similar to typeof(), but it is less precise.

## Part C — Type Conversion (20 min)
R can convert (coerce) values between types using functions like as.numeric(), as.integer(), as.character(), and as.logical().

```{r}
num_string <- "123"
as.numeric(num_string)
num_string
typeof(num_string)
class(num_string)
mode(num_string)
```
It does not convert to numeric, it displays character in the console.

```{r}
as.logical(0)
as.logical(1)
```
For the logical(0), it displays false and for the logical(1), it displays true. This is because 0 is considered false and 1 is considered true in programming.

```{r}
bad_string <- "hello123"
as.numeric(bad_string)
bad_string
```
A warning displayed "NAs introduced by coercion" and the result is "hello123".

I think crashing the whole script is unnecessary and not useful when it comes to coding, that is why R is designed to only give a warning and not crash the whole script or else everything would be gone in an instant.

Warning are there for a reason, they help you check whether or not you did something wrong. Not reading warnings can result to more errors in the future.

Question #6: as.logical(0) and as.logical(1) convert to FALSE and TRUE.

### What do you think as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1)` will produce?

Both as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1) will produce 2.

R seems to follow the non-zero rule on the logical area since if the value is 0 it is considered false.

## Part D — Strings, paste(), and paste0()
Strings are stored as the character type. paste() joins strings with a space separator by default; paste0() joins them with no separator.

```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"
cat(first_name, last_name)
```
It prints both of it together with the use of cat().

```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"
paste(first_name, last_name)
paste0(first_name, last_name)

```
paste() puts blank spaces while paste0() does not use blanks.

```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"
paste(first_name, last_name, sep = "-")
```
The argument uses - instead of a blank space.

```{r}
full_name <- "Juan Dela Cruz"
age <- "21 years old"
text <- "is"
paste(full_name, text, age)

```
paste() combined all my variables and created a sentence.

Question #7: paste() and paste0() produced different results for the same two strings. Explain exactly why, referencing what each function does by default.

paste() uses a blank space to combine characters, while paste0() does not use blank spaces when combining characters.

Question #8: In the strings-numbers chunk, you combined a character string with a numeric variable (age) using paste0() without first converting age to a string.

### Did this cause an error? Explain what paste0() does internally to make this work, and how it relates to the type conversions you practiced in Part C.

The paste0() function in R is designed to handle different data types automatically. When you pass a numeric variable like age into paste0(), R automatically performs an internal implicit type coercion. It converts the numeric value into a character string before concatenating it with the other text.

Question #9: Some programming languages automatically convert "5" + 5 into 10 without an error. R does not.

### Based on what you’ve learned about R’s data types in this lab, why do you think R requires an explicit conversion instead of guessing what the programmer meant?

In R, strict data type safety and the prevention of silent errors are the primary reasons why the language requires explicit conversion instead of guessing the programmer's intent.

Question #10: Suppose a classmate writes a script that reads a column of “numbers” from a text file. The column looks numeric, but when they try sum() on it, R throws an error. Based on everything in this lab (types, typeof()/class()/mode(), conversion, warnings), write a short paragraph explaining what likely went wrong and the steps you’d take to diagnose and fix it.

The error likely occurred because R imported the column as a character vector or a factor, rather than a numeric vector

# Conclusion
In R, data types like logical, integer, double, and character tells you how information is stored and processed. R uses implicit coercion during arithmetic operations, often quietly turning logical values into numbers or throwing errors if characters are involved. Understanding typeof() and class() matters because it allows you to verify the exact structure of your data before manipulating it, preventing unexpected behavior. Master functions like as.numeric() or as.character() ensures that data combinations and calculations yield predictable, accurate results without breaking your workflows.
